questions.q: Why can't an experienced engineer reliably answer "what's actually affected if this service fails" from memory in an enterprise estate with dozens of interdependent services?
options: The scale of real dependency chains across dozens of services exceeds what anyone can hold accurately in their head, no matter how senior or tenured they are
Enterprise services never have more than one dependency each, so memory should actually be sufficient
This is only a problem for services that have never been documented at all
Distributed tracing makes human knowledge of dependencies unnecessary from day one
questions.explain: At real enterprise scale, no one can correctly hold the full dependency graph in their head, which is why a current, queryable service catalog and dependency graph have to replace that mental model.

questions.q: What does a real service catalog need to track, beyond a service's name and owner, to actually support DR decisions?
options: Only the programming language the service is written in
Its DR tier, RTO/RPO, and an explicit, current list of what it calls and what calls it
Only its deployment region, since dependencies rarely matter for failover
Only its git repository URL
questions.explain: A useful service catalog tracks DR tier, RTO/RPO, and both upstream and downstream dependencies, kept current — that's what makes it possible to answer real blast-radius and failover-coordination questions.

questions.q: Why can distributed tracing reveal dependencies that a diligently maintained architecture diagram misses?
options: Tracing observes what the system actually does in real traffic, catching couplings like an undocumented "temporary" synchronous call that was never removed and never added to the diagram
Architecture diagrams are always generated automatically from tracing data, so this scenario cannot occur
Tracing only works for services written in the same programming language
Documentation is always more accurate than tracing, so this is a hypothetical concern
questions.explain: People document what they intended to build, not always what actually shipped; tracing follows real requests across service boundaries and surfaces couplings — like an undocumented call into a legacy dependency — that documentation alone missed.

questions.q: What does it mean that blast radius is the "transitive closure" of a dependency graph rather than just the first hop out?
options: Blast radius only includes services in the same cloud region as the failed service
Blast radius includes every node reachable by following dependency edges outward through multiple hops, not just the services that call the failed service directly
Blast radius is limited to exactly two hops from the point of failure, by definition
Transitive closure is a billing term unrelated to dependency graphs
questions.explain: A failure's real blast radius includes everything reachable through the graph — direct callers, their callers, and so on outward — not just the services that call the failed service directly.

questions.q: Why does an accurate dependency graph need to exist before a failover decision ships, rather than being useful only after the fact?
options: Because failing over a service without accounting for everything actually downstream of it is how Lesson 13's boundary failure happens repeatedly and simultaneously across a large estate
Dependency graphs are only useful for billing and cost allocation, not for failover decisions
A failover decision never needs to consider any service besides the one that failed
Because regulators require a dependency graph to be filed before any failover, regardless of its accuracy
questions.explain: Without an accurate graph, a failover decision can't account for everything actually affected, which is exactly how a boundary failure like the checkout/pricing example in Lesson 13 recurs at scale across an estate.
